theme: The first journey concludes; Lystra and Derbe
readingInstruction: Read Acts 14:1-28. Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe. They heal a man, are mistaken for gods, and Paul is stoned. They return, strengthening the churches and appointing elders. Read Paul’s speech at Lystra (vv. 15 to 17) carefully.
settingTheScene: The first missionary journey continues from Pisidian Antioch to Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, cities in what is now central Turkey. The pattern is that Paul first speaks in the synagogue, the Gentiles respond, and the Jews stir up opposition. At Lystra there is no synagogue, and the population is pagan, so Paul’s message begins with God as Creator, a template for preaching to those with no biblical background.
observation: “So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace” (14:3).
“The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” (14:11).

“We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them” (14:15).
“Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (14:17).
“They stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead” (14:19).
“Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (14:22).
“And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed” (14:23).
“They declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles” (14:27).
interpretation:
In Iconium, a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, but unbelieving Jews stir up the Gentiles. Paul and Barnabas stay a long time, speaking boldly, with signs and wonders, and then flee when a plot to stone them arises.

At Lystra, Paul sees a man crippled from birth who has faith to be made well, and says, “Stand upright on your feet.” The man leaps up and walks. The crowd shouts in their local language, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and the priest of Zeus brings oxen and garlands to offer sacrifice. Paul and Barnabas tear their garments and rush into the crowd: “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you.” Their message is not about themselves but about the living God: “turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea.” Though in past generations God allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways, he has not left himself without witness, giving rain and fruitful seasons, satisfying hearts with food and gladness. This is the first example in Acts of preaching to people with no Scriptural background. Paul starts with creation, God’s goodness, and the folly of idolatry, and only later comes to Christ. Even so, they can scarcely restrain the people from sacrificing.

Then Jews arrive from Antioch and Iconium, win over the crowds, and stone Paul and drag him out of the city, thinking him dead. The people who wanted to worship him now try to kill him. But as the disciples gather around him, he gets up and goes back into the city. The next day he leaves for Derbe.

They return the way they came, strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” They appoint elders in every church, with prayer and fasting. Back in Antioch, they report “all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.” It is God who opens the door and God who does the work.
connection: Genesis 1 and Psalm 146:6 describe God as the maker of heaven and earth. Psalm 145:15-16 says he satisfies the desire of every living thing. Romans 1:18-23 and 2:14-15 describe general revelation. Acts 17:22-31 is Paul’s similar speech in Athens. 2 Corinthians 11:25 recalls the stoning. 2 Timothy 3:11 mentions his sufferings at Lystra. Titus 1:5 shows Titus appointing elders. John 16:33 says in the world you will have tribulation.
application:
Practice explaining the gospel to someone with no Christian background, starting with creation.

Remember that tribulation is not a sign you’re off track. It is part of the road to the kingdom.

Thank God for the elders in your church, and pray for them.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for his goodness in rain, seasons, food, and gladness.
Ask him to keep you from taking his glory.
Ask him to strengthen believers who face hardship.
